metaData.originalTitle: My dad bragged online about sexually abusing me. But he was making it all up
metaData.title: My dad bragged online about sexually abusing me. But he was making it all up
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: A woman recounts how her father was arrested for allegedly sexually abusing her after fantasizing about it online—only for the charges to be dropped due to a legal loophole, sparking her campaign for law reform.
metaData.summary: This Guardian feature tells the story of Emily, whose father Mark was arrested after an undercover police officer discovered him describing detailed fantasies of sexually abusing her in online chat rooms. Despite Emily’s insistence that the abuse never happened, the police pursued charges for indecent communication. However, the Crown Prosecution Service dropped the case, arguing that because Mark’s messages were shared privately with an apparently like-minded recipient, they could not prove the material was intended to be indecent or obscene. The article follows Emily and her mother Fiona through the shock of the arrest, the unraveling of their family, and Emily’s subsequent determination to challenge the legal gap. It includes expert commentary from law professor Clare McGlynn and child abuse expert Michael Sheath, who argue that such fantasy chat normalizes and escalates interest in child abuse. Emily’s advocacy—meeting with her MP and the minister for victims—has contributed to recent legislative amendments banning step-incest pornography and performer role-playing as children, but a specific offence for text-based advocacy of child sexual abuse remains absent.

mainPoints.point: Fantasy child abuse chat can be legally protected if shared privately between like-minded participants.
mainPoints.explanation: The CPS dropped charges against Mark because the messages were exchanged in a private chat with a recipient who responded in kind, making it hard to prove intent to deprave or corrupt under the Obscene Publications Act.

mainPoints.point: Victims of fantasy abuse face unique trauma and lack legal recognition.
mainPoints.explanation: Emily was told by police that she was not a victim under the law—the 'victim' was the undercover officer who read the messages. This caused lasting psychological harm and dissociation.

mainPoints.point: Experts warn that online fantasy chat normalizes and escalates child abuse interest.
mainPoints.explanation: Clare McGlynn and Michael Sheath explain that community chat creates an echo chamber where boundaries are pushed, encouraging real-world abuse.

mainPoints.point: Emily’s personal advocacy spurred legislative change but a legal gap remains.
mainPoints.explanation: Amendments to the Crime and Policing Act now ban step-incest and adult-performer child role-play in porn, but no specific offence covers written advocacy of child sexual abuse.

keyQuotes: He was an ordinary man. A good dad. There aren't signs and no one should be expected to spot them before it happens.
I get why people ask if I'm sure he didn't abuse me. But this isn't just a random, unusual thing; it happens all the time.
Once you are in that space, you will learn you aren't alone; other people will encourage your sexual interest in children.
